newsitem.title: USA: Heat wave seen next week in southern U.S. Plains.
newsitem.headline: Heat wave seen next week in southern U.S. Plains.

text.p: Temperatures next week in Texas and Oklahoma will likely soar above the 100 degree Fahrenheit mark as a heat wave hits the southern U.S. Plains, forecasters said Friday.

Jeff Penner, a meteorologist at the Weather Center Co in Kansas City, said a dome of heat will form next week over New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana. The heat will stick around over the first six to 10 days of July, he said.
Penner said that while heat waves in July in Texas were not uncommon, next week's heat could "go the extra mile" if conditions are right.
"If it's clear and the dome is without clouds...it could be 100 to 110 (degrees F) in Dallas and in Lubbock, and the cotton areas of west Texas could really broil," Penner said.
Meteorologists were unsure how far north the heat wave would spread.
Fred Gesser, Weather Express Inc meteorologist, said weather models showed the heat wave lasting at least through July 10 and possibly until July 15.
Gesser said there was a possibility that temperatures in the upper 90s and 100s Fahrenheit would extend north next week from central Texas into western Kansas.
But Penner said the central Plains could experience strong thunderstorms next week because the area would be trapped between two weather systems.

At the same time the dome of heat is forming in the southern Plains, a strong trough will form in the Great Lakes and in southern Canada, Penner said. In between, a very fast-moving jet stream will flow from southern Kansas through the western Corn Belt.
"This will set up what we call a 'rim of fire' pattern, meaning that thunderstorms rim the periphery of the dome," Penner said.

"The line right now, based on our data, is on the Oklahoma-Kansas border, so that would put Kansas, Nebraska and Colorado in the rim of fire -- in the thunderstorms -- starting Monday night," Penner said.
